title: SpO2 Below 94% Threshold
interpretation: Blood oxygen saturation below 94% at rest is considered clinically significant. Normal SpO2 is 95-100%. Values between 90-94% indicate mild hypoxemia. Below 90% is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention. Altitude, COPD, and sleep apnea can cause chronically lower baseline SpO2.
recommended_agent_action: If SpO2 drops below 94% for more than 2 consecutive readings at rest, escalate to Level 4. Cross-reference with breathing rate and heart rate. If below 90%, escalate to Level 5.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose respiratory failure or pneumonia. Wearable SpO2 sensors have accuracy limitations of ±2%. Cold fingers or poor sensor contact can cause false low readings.

title: Nocturnal Oxygen Desaturation
interpretation: SpO2 drops during sleep that fall below 90% or show a pattern of repetitive desaturation-resaturation cycles are suggestive of sleep-disordered breathing. The combination of SpO2 dips and elevated breathing rate during sleep strengthens this association. Normal nocturnal SpO2 remains above 93%.
recommended_agent_action: Track nocturnal SpO2 patterns. If repetitive dips below 93% occur on multiple nights, flag as potential sleep-disordered breathing and suggest sleep study discussion with doctor.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose sleep apnea from SpO2 data alone. A formal polysomnography is required for diagnosis.
sources: American Academy of Sleep Medicine - Oximetry

title: Elevated Resting Breathing Rate
interpretation: Normal resting breathing rate is 12-20 breaths per minute. A sustained rate above 20 at rest (tachypnea) may indicate respiratory distress, anxiety, pain, metabolic acidosis, or fever. Above 25 at rest is more concerning. Context is critical: recent exercise, anxiety, and speaking patterns affect rate.
recommended_agent_action: If resting breathing rate exceeds 20 for multiple consecutive readings while sedentary, cross-reference with SpO2, HR, and stress indicators. Escalate if SpO2 is also declining.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose respiratory conditions from breathing rate alone. Many benign factors temporarily elevate breathing rate.
sources: Lancet - Respiratory Rate as Vital Sign

title: Acute Respiratory Distress Pattern
interpretation: Simultaneous SpO2 drop below 93%, breathing rate above 22, and heart rate elevation while sedentary at night creates a critical triad suggesting acute respiratory distress. In elderly users, this pattern has higher clinical significance and warrants immediate attention regardless of other context.
recommended_agent_action: Immediate Level 5 alert. This combination, especially in elderly or users with known respiratory conditions, requires immediate notification and emergency contact alert.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, or heart failure. The pattern indicates distress requiring professional evaluation.

title: SpO2 Decline with Temperature Rise
interpretation: Gradual SpO2 decline (from normal to 94-95%) concurrent with rising skin temperature above baseline suggests possible respiratory infection. The body's metabolic demand increases with fever, while respiratory efficiency may decrease due to infection. This is an early illness indicator.
recommended_agent_action: Track SpO2 and temperature trend together. If both are moving in concerning directions for 2+ days, flag as possible illness onset and recommend monitoring.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose infection or COVID-19. Temperature and SpO2 changes have many possible causes.
sources: Journal of Medical Internet Research - Wearable Illness Detection

title: Stress-Induced Hyperventilation
interpretation: Elevated breathing rate above 22 concurrent with high stress scores but normal SpO2 and normal heart rate suggests stress-induced hyperventilation rather than respiratory pathology. Hyperventilation maintains or even increases SpO2 while causing symptoms like dizziness, tingling, and chest tightness.
recommended_agent_action: If breathing rate is elevated but SpO2 is normal or high (98-100%), this is likely stress-related. Suggest breathing exercises. Do not escalate as respiratory emergency.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not assume hyperventilation is harmless. Chronic hyperventilation syndrome requires treatment. Also do not dismiss respiratory rate changes solely as stress.

title: Exercise-Induced Oxygen Desaturation
interpretation: SpO2 dropping below 95% during intense exercise occurs in some healthy individuals, especially at altitude or during extreme exertion. However, significant desaturation below 92% during moderate exercise may indicate exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or cardiovascular limitation.
recommended_agent_action: Log exercise SpO2 patterns. If desaturation below 92% occurs during moderate exercise repeatedly, suggest discussing with healthcare provider.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose exercise-induced asthma or cardiac limitation from wearable SpO2 during exercise. Motion artifacts significantly affect accuracy during activity.
sources: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise - SpO2

title: Persistent Nocturnal Low SpO2
interpretation: SpO2 consistently remaining at 93-94% during sleep across multiple nights, even without dramatic desaturation cycles, may indicate chronic low-grade nocturnal hypoxemia. This can be associated with obesity hypoventilation, COPD, or living at altitude. Long-term consequences include pulmonary hypertension.
recommended_agent_action: If nocturnal SpO2 baseline is consistently at 93-94% for 7+ nights, recommend medical evaluation. Frame as precautionary check, not emergency.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose chronic respiratory disease. Wearable SpO2 accuracy during sleep is lower than clinical pulse oximetry.
sources: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine - Nocturnal Hypoxemia
